title: Mastery Challenge: World Religions
objective: After this level you can demonstrate command of World Religions Levels 1 to 99 across the whole tree.
summary: Ten questions from across the tree: defining, describing and counting religions, families of faith, secular states, doubt, conflict, new movements and dialogue.

cards.headline: The World Religions Mastery Challenge.
cards.body: Questions from across the whole tree, from how scholars define religion to how people of different faiths talk to each other. Take your time: every question can be corrected.

cards.headline: World Religions: mastered
learned: How scholars describe any religion fairly, through its practices and stories as well as its beliefs.
Why every tradition speaks with many voices, and how to test claims about any faith.
How believers and the unaffiliated are counted, and why 'none' rarely means no belief.
How secular states, fair scholarship and interfaith dialogue make room for many faiths.

questions.prompt: About what share of the world's people were religiously unaffiliated in 2020?

options.label: About 4%
options.rationale: That was roughly the Buddhist share.

options.label: About 15%
options.rationale: That was roughly the Hindu share.

options.label: About 29%
options.rationale: That was roughly the Christian share.

questions.explanation: About 24% of the world was religiously unaffiliated in 2020, third after Christians and Muslims.

questions.prompt: You want to describe a faith you've never studied without reducing it to its beliefs. Whose checklist gives you rituals, stories, ethics, community and sacred places too?

options.label: Edward Tylor's
options.rationale: Tylor offered a one-line definition, not a checklist.

options.label: Arnold van Gennep's three stages
options.rationale: Those describe rites of passage only.

options.label: William James's four marks
options.rationale: Those describe mystical states only.

questions.explanation: Smart's seven dimensions cover ritual, experience, narrative, doctrine, ethics, the social side and the material side.

questions.prompt: At a graduation, students leave their seats, cross the stage, then rejoin their families as graduates. Which of van Gennep's stages is the walk across the stage?

options.label: Separation
options.rationale: That's leaving the seats, the old status.

options.label: Incorporation
options.rationale: That's rejoining the families as graduates.

options.label: Revelation
options.rationale: That isn't one of van Gennep's stages.

questions.explanation: The middle stage, transition, is the threshold: out of the old status, not yet in the new one.

questions.prompt: Who built the carved stone pillars of Göbekli Tepe?

options.label: Hunter-gatherers who had not yet taken up farming
Roman engineers
options.rationale: The site is far older than Rome.

options.label: Early city dwellers with writing
options.rationale: It predates writing by thousands of years.

options.label: Medieval monks
options.rationale: It dates to the 10th to 9th millennium BCE.

questions.explanation: People who had not yet taken up farming raised Göbekli Tepe in the 10th to 9th millennium BCE.

questions.prompt: Karma, rebirth and the hope of release from rebirth run through which family of faiths?

options.label: The Abrahamic family
options.rationale: That family traces itself to Abraham.

options.label: The East Asian family
options.rationale: That family draws on Confucian, Daoist and Buddhist traditions and Shinto.

options.label: The Indigenous traditions
options.rationale: Those are many traditions, each tied to its own people and land.

questions.explanation: Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism and Sikhism, the Indian family, share ideas of karma, samsara and moksha.

questions.prompt: Which two rules does the First Amendment set for religion in the United States?

options.label: A state church, and freedom to leave it
options.rationale: The amendment forbids an established church.

options.label: No established religion, and free exercise for all
Equal funding for every faith, and religious family law
options.rationale: That's closer to India's model.

options.label: No religious symbols in schools, and no state recognition
options.rationale: That's France's laïcité.

questions.explanation: Congress may make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting its free exercise.

questions.prompt: Which statement about American religious nones fits Pew's findings?

options.label: Nearly all nones are committed atheists
options.rationale: Atheists are about 17% of nones.

options.label: Nones never think of themselves as spiritual
options.rationale: About half do.

options.label: Most believe in God or some other higher power
Nones make up most of the US population
options.rationale: They were 29% of adults in 2023-24.

questions.explanation: Most nones believe in God or another higher power; 'none' rarely means no belief at all.

questions.prompt: What do Juergensmeyer and Cavanaugh agree on about conflicts called religious?

options.label: Religion is the root cause of most wars
options.rationale: Neither argues this.

options.label: Religious language plays no part in them
options.rationale: Juergensmeyer says it supplies justification and meaning.

options.label: Only secular states avoid them
options.rationale: Neither makes that claim.

questions.explanation: Juergensmeyer points to social, political and economic causes; Cavanaugh to power and a slippery category. Neither treats faith as the whole story.

questions.prompt: Which pair of tools lets you study a controversial new religious movement fairly?

options.label: Count its members, then rank it against older faiths
options.rationale: Scholars describe; they don't rank.

options.label: Label it a cult, then look for evidence
options.rationale: That builds the conclusion into the definition.

options.label: Judge it by its founder's beliefs alone
options.rationale: Barker separates the movement, its leaders and its members.

options.label: Bracket the question of truth, and judge it by what it does

questions.explanation: Level 4's bracketing sets truth aside; Barker's rule judges a movement by what it believes and does, here and now.

questions.prompt: The 1893 World's Parliament of Religions is regarded as the origin of what?

options.label: The study of rites of passage
options.rationale: Van Gennep named those in 1909.

options.label: The secularization thesis
options.rationale: Berger set that out in 1967.

options.label: France's separation law
options.rationale: That was France's 1905 law.

questions.explanation: The 1893 Parliament in Chicago is regarded as the origin of the modern interfaith movement.
